title: Power struggles: what the Middle East conflict means for European power markets
gist: Wood Mackenzie's base case is that the Middle East conflict does not significantly alter European power market fundamentals, but Brian Gaylord lays out two alternative scenarios: a Summer Settlement where Hormuz reopens by end-summer and adds €13/MWh to 2027 power prices, and an Extended Disruption where the Strait reopens only at end-2026, average European power prices run about €45/MWh above base through 2027, gas and power prices do not recouple with base case until 2038, and a short recession wipes out €500 billion of annual European GDP. Italy and Ireland see the largest price impact given high gas import dependence, but prices stay below the post-Ukraine-invasion peaks, lowering the odds of 2022-23 style market interventions.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's May 2026 long-term outlook base case holds that the Middle East conflict will not significantly alter European power market fundamentals despite creating meaningful short-term risk.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: The house view is that this is a price event, not a structural break — sets the anchor against which the two stress scenarios should be read.
insights.quote: our base-case scenario ‒ that the Middle East conflict will not significantly alter European power market fundamentals, despite creating meaningful short-term risk
insights.locator: To supplement our May 2026 long-term outlook

insights.claim: The critical variable separating Wood Mackenzie's two Middle East stress scenarios for European power is consumer reaction to a lengthy uplift in gas prices, not the gas price level itself.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Watch behavioural indicators — heat pump and EV adoption rates — rather than gas forwards to judge which scenario Europe is tracking.
insights.quote: The critical difference between our two new modelled scenarios is consumers’ reaction to a lengthy uplift in gas prices.
insights.locator: How could disruption to the Strait of Hormuz affect European gas and power markets?

insights.claim: The European gas market was already tight before the disruption to Middle East supply, so the Hormuz closure compounds a pre-existing imbalance rather than creating one.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: A reopening of Hormuz alone does not restore balance — the underlying tightness persists and limits downside in European gas.
insights.quote: The European gas market was already tight before the disruption to Middle East supply.
insights.locator: How could disruption to the Strait of Hormuz affect European gas and power markets?

insights.claim: The longer the Strait of Hormuz remains closed, the higher gas prices rise and the greater the potential for European electricity prices to remain elevated — a direct duration-to-price transmission.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Closure duration, not closure severity, is the variable to track for European power price forecasts.
insights.quote: The longer the Strait remains closed, the higher gas prices will rise and the greater the potential for electricity prices to remain elevated.
insights.locator: How could disruption to the Strait of Hormuz affect European gas and power markets?

insights.claim: Under Wood Mackenzie's Summer Settlement scenario, Strait of Hormuz traffic is resolved by the end of summer 2026, LNG shipments resume in September and ramp up slowly, with regional tensions persisting but no escalation.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: The benign case still assumes a slow LNG ramp, meaning even resolution does not deliver immediate supply relief.

insights.claim: The Summer Settlement scenario adds €13/MWh to Wood Mackenzie's base-case European power price outlook in 2027, with the fuel adjustment limited to higher pricing between 2026 and 2029 and recoupling with the base case in 2030.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Quantifies the mild case at +€13/MWh for 2027 — a benchmark for pricing European power PPAs and utility earnings sensitivity.
insights.quote: This scenario would add €13/MWh to our base-case outlook in 2027.
insights.locator: The fuel adjustment is largely limited to higher pricing

insights.claim: Under the Summer Settlement scenario European electricity demand stays the same as the base case, because near-term conflict resolution produces minimal policy intervention and any additional electrification is minimal or offset by losses.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Quick resolution means no acceleration in electrification demand — bad for the heat pump and EV supply-chain acceleration thesis.
insights.locator: European electricity demand remains the same as in our base case

insights.claim: Under Wood Mackenzie's Extended Disruption scenario, passage through the Strait of Hormuz is reinstated only at the end of 2026, the global LNG market is fundamentally reshaped, gas supply is lower, demand destruction occurs and prices are more volatile.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: The stress case reshapes global LNG structurally, not just European prices — relevant to long-dated LNG contracting and liquefaction FIDs.
insights.quote: In this scenario, the global LNG market is fundamentally reshaped, gas supply is lower, demand destruction occurs and prices are more volatile.

insights.claim: In the Extended Disruption scenario European fuel prices diverge from the base case and do not recouple until 2038, a twelve-year divergence from a roughly one-year physical disruption.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: A one-year chokepoint closure permanently repricing the curve to 2038 is the key non-obvious result — far-dated European power and gas curves are the mispriced part.
insights.quote: Fuel prices diverge from our base case and do not recouple until 2038.
insights.locator: Fuel prices diverge from our base case

insights.claim: The Extended Disruption scenario assumes an economic recession in the second half of 2026 that cuts base electricity demand, with European GDP returning to pre-crisis levels in 2027 but €500 billion of annual GDP permanently wiped out.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: €500 billion of lost annual European GDP is the macro number to carry into European equity and rates views under a prolonged Hormuz closure.
insights.quote: The recession is short lived, with European gross domestic product (GDP) returning to pre-crisis levels in 2027, but €500 billion of annual GDP is wiped out, undermining base electricity demand.
insights.locator: An economic recession in the second half of 2026

insights.claim: Average European power prices run approximately €45/MWh above base case by the end of 2026 and throughout 2027 under the Extended Disruption scenario, before easing by 2031.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: +€45/MWh for two years is the headline stress number for European power offtakers, industrials and utility hedging books.
insights.quote: average European power prices are around €45/MWh higher than in our base case by the end of 2026 and throughout 2027, before easing by 2031
insights.locator: Under the Extended Disruption scenario, average European power prices

insights.claim: Prolonged gas supply disruption raises European power prices by €50/MWh in the near term before demand destruction pulls prices back to base-case levels by 2030 under Summer Settlement and further below by the mid-2030s under Extended Disruption.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: The stress case is bullish near-dated and bearish far-dated European power — an argued case for a steep inverted power curve.
insights.quote: The prolonged disruption of gas supply raises prices by €50/MWh in the near-term, before demand destruction lowers prices to base-case levels by 2030
insights.locator: What is the European power price outlook if LNG supply remains constrained?

insights.claim: Sustained LNG disruption ultimately leads to gas demand destruction because the transport and heating sectors accelerate electrification to insulate themselves from fossil-fuel transport interruptions.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: The crisis is a structural accelerant for electrification demand — bullish for heat pumps, EVs and grid capex, bearish for long-run European gas volumes.
insights.quote: This would ultimately lead to gas demand destruction as the transport and heating sectors accelerate electrification in a bid to ward off the consequences of interruptions to fossil-fuel transport.
insights.locator: Any sustained disruption to vessel traffic

insights.claim: Under the Extended Disruption scenario the adoption of electric vehicles and heat pumps is brought forward as consumers move away from fossil fuels to avoid higher costs, permanently reshaping European power demand.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: A prolonged Hormuz closure is a demand-pull catalyst for EV and heat pump manufacturers, offsetting the recessionary hit to their end markets.
insights.quote: the adoption of electric vehicles and heat pumps is brought forward as consumers move away from fossil fuels to avoid higher costs
insights.locator: An economic recession in the second half of 2026

insights.claim: Italy and Ireland are likely to see the greatest power price impact under the Extended Disruption scenario because of their high dependence on gas imports.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Names the two most exposed national markets — relevant for country-level power hedging, utility selection and industrial cost exposure.
insights.quote: Italy and Ireland are likely to see the greatest impact on power prices under our Extended Disruption scenario thanks to their high dependence on gas imports.
insights.locator: Italy and Ireland are likely to see the greatest impact

insights.claim: Exposure to fuel cost increases raises market power prices across Europe by between €33/MWh and €19/MWh over the initial five years of the Extended Disruption case.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Gives a five-year regional uplift band of €19-33/MWh for modelling European power capture prices and generator margins.
insights.quote: Exposure to fuel cost increases raises market power prices across the region between €33/MWh and €19 /MWh over the initial five years of our Extended Disruption case.
insights.locator: Italy and Ireland are likely to see the greatest impact

insights.claim: Even in the Extended Disruption scenario European power prices remain below the peaks experienced after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, reducing the probability of market interventions akin to those seen in 2022-23.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Windfall taxes and price caps are less likely than the 2022 analogue implies — a meaningful de-risking for European utility and generator earnings.
insights.quote: even in this scenario, power prices remain below the peaks experienced after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, reducing the probability of market interventions akin to those seen in 2022-23
insights.locator: However, even in this scenario, power prices remain below the peaks

insights.claim: Recurring ceasefire breakdowns and misaligned US-Israeli objectives continue to make a durable Middle East peace agreement and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz elusive, prolonging uncertainty over LNG vessel passage.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Attributes the persistence of the disruption to structural allied misalignment, not a single negotiation — implying a longer risk premium than headline-driven pricing assumes.
insights.quote: Recurring ceasefire breakdowns and misaligned US–Israeli objectives continue to ensure that a durable Middle East peace agreement and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz remain elusive.
insights.locator: Recurring ceasefire breakdowns and misaligned US–Israeli objectives
